It favors columns with many distinct values, so a customer ID with no signal ranked second, and a binary feature that really matters ranked last. Use permutation importance on held-out data, and group correlated features before you read it.
A churn team plots its random forest's feature importances for a planning meeting. Tenure in days tops the chart, then
, then tenure in months and support calls;

comes last. Someone suggests that older accounts, with lower IDs, might churn differently, and the contract offer the product team wanted drops down the roadmap. Both conclusions come from the chart, and both are wrong: the ID carries no information at all, and the contract flag is one of the two features the model leans on most for new customers.

items.text: It comes free with every fitted forest, sums to 1 and sorts into a clean bar chart.
It's computed from the model's own splits, so it feels like an inside view of how the model decides.
On well-behaved data it often agrees with intuition, which builds trust in the cases where it shouldn't.

content.text: The half-truth: it does describe the trained forest, which columns the trees split on and how much each split reduced impurity on the training rows. But that's a record of fitting, including overfitting, not a measure of predictive value on data the model hasn't seen.
There are two common ways to score a feature, and they answer different questions.
Impurity importance counts splits on training rows

(MDI), adds up how much each feature's splits reduced impurity across all trees. scikit-learn's permutation importance example gives two reasons it misleads: it's biased toward high-cardinality features, and it's computed on training set statistics, so it doesn't reflect what generalizes. A column with 1,500 distinct values offers up to 1,499 candidate split points; a binary column offers one. Each split is chosen to look best on the training rows, so the column with more chances finds splits that fit noise, especially deep in the tree where nodes are small. Strobl and colleagues traced the bias in random forests to this biased split selection, plus effects of bootstrap sampling.
Permutation importance measures lost accuracy on new rows

shuffles one column at a time and records how much the model's score drops. Computed on a held-out set, it asks the question you actually have: how much does the model rely on this column for predictions that generalize? tabs.label: ❌ Wrong
tabs.code:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 2000
months = rng.integers(1, 72, n)
X = np.column_stack([months,
                     months * 30 + rng.integers(0, 30, n),  # tenure in days
                     rng.poisson(1.5, n),     # support calls
                     rng.integers(0, 2, n),   # has a contract
                     rng.permutation(n)])     # customer ID: no signal
names = ["tenure_months", "tenure_days", "support_calls", "has_contract",
         "customer_id"]
logit = 0.5 - 0.04 * X[:, 0] + 0.6 * X[:, 2] - 1.5 * X[:, 3]
y = (rng.random(n) < 1 / (1 + np.exp(-logit))).astype(int)  # churned
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X, y, stratify=y, random_state=0)
rf = RandomForestClassifier(random_state=0).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
for name, mdi in zip(names, rf.feature_importances_):
    print(f"{name:14} {mdi:.3f}")
# tenure_months  0.188
# tenure_days    0.321
# support_calls  0.122
# has_contract   0.084
# customer_id    0.285

tabs.label: ✅ Right
tabs.code:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.inspection import permutation_importance
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 2000
months = rng.integers(1, 72, n)
X = np.column_stack([months, months * 30 + rng.integers(0, 30, n),
                     rng.poisson(1.5, n), rng.integers(0, 2, n),
                     rng.permutation(n)])
names = ["tenure_months", "tenure_days", "support_calls", "has_contract",
         "customer_id"]
logit = 0.5 - 0.04 * X[:, 0] + 0.6 * X[:, 2] - 1.5 * X[:, 3]
y = (rng.random(n) < 1 / (1 + np.exp(-logit))).astype(int)
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X, y, stratify=y, random_state=0)
rf = RandomForestClassifier(random_state=0).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
pi = permutation_importance(rf, X_te, y_te, n_repeats=10, random_state=0)
for name, m, s in zip(names, pi.importances_mean, pi.importances_std):
    print(f"{name:14} {m:+.3f} +/- {s:.3f}")
# tenure_months  +0.001 +/- 0.008
# tenure_days    +0.013 +/- 0.010
# support_calls  +0.040 +/- 0.012
# has_contract   +0.040 +/- 0.015
# customer_id    -0.015 +/- 0.012

content.text: The impurity ranking follows the number of distinct values almost exactly:
2. On held-out data the picture flips. Shuffling

costs nothing, −0.015 ± 0.012, which is noise around zero, while support calls and the contract flag, last in the impurity chart, are the model's two most relied-on features, each worth 0.040 of accuracy.
The forest really does use the ID, though. It scores 1.000 on its training rows and 0.69 on the test rows, and on the training rows shuffling

costs 0.184 of accuracy. The model memorized customers by ID. The permutation guide uses exactly this comparison: features that matter on the training set but not on held-out data may be causing the model to overfit.

Now look at tenure. It drives churn in this data, yet both tenure columns score near zero: +0.001 and +0.013. Shuffling one leaves the other intact, so the model barely notices. The guide warns about exactly this: when two features are correlated, permuting one leaves the information available through the other, which lowers the importance of both even if they matter. Drop

rises to +0.030. scikit-learn's multicollinear example shows the extreme case: on the breast cancer data, a forest scores about 97% on the test set, yet permuting any single feature drops training accuracy by at most 0.012. Its fix is to cluster features by rank correlation and keep one per cluster.

blocks.title: Compare training and held-out permutation importance

content.text: on both sets. A feature that matters on the training rows but not on held-out rows is being used to overfit, like the ID here. Before reading any importance, check the model's held-out score: the guide warns that a feature unimportant to a bad model can be very important to a good one.

blocks.title: Don't drop features by low permutation importance alone

content.text: If a column scores near zero, check whether a correlated column is covering for it before you remove it. Remove both twins and the model loses the information the scores said it didn't need. Group correlated features first, then judge the group.
How to apply it in your project
Measure its held-out score with cross-validation. Importances of a model that doesn't generalize describe noise.

Large gaps between training and held-out importance point to features the model uses to memorize.
Group columns by rank correlation, as in scikit-learn's multicollinear example, and judge or drop whole groups.
Write "the model relies on support calls", not "support calls drive churn"; importance describes the model, not cause and effect.

items.text: Impurity importance comes from training splits and favors many distinct values: a no-signal ID ranked second.
Permutation importance on held-out data measures what the model needs for new predictions.
A feature important on training rows but not held-out ones is being used to overfit.
Correlated features share and hide credit; group them before you trust or drop anything.
